title: 3  Central Tendency
text:
The mean
The mean, or average, is more nuanced because it uses every numerical value, not only their ordered positions. To calculate it, we add all the scores and then divide by the number of scores. This might seem like a simple idea, and we’ll soon see what’s so elegant and useful about it. But it took a long time to catch on. It’s worth taking a brief historical tour of the idea to get a sense of its uses (and abuses).
Averaging, as a mathematical idea, has been around for a long time. The Pythagoreans discussed it in the third century BCE, but in the context of musical theory rather than data analysis. You would think scientists whose job involves taking multiple observations and figuring out what to make of them would have been quick to adopt the mean for their purposes, but it took a while. Astronomy provides an extensive historical record (see Raper, 2017). As long ago as the second century BCE, the Greek astronomer Hipparchus was observing the positions of celestial bodies, recording things like times, angles, and distances.



Figure 3.4: A sixteenth-century illustration of Hipparchus, anachronistically using the sort of quadrant familiar to a sixteenth-century illustrator. There was some clever equipment in Hipparchus’s day; he wasn’t exactly just eyeballing things, but there was plenty of room for measurement error.1






Hipparchus and other astronomers realized that of course any one observation could be a bit off, so there’s value in combining multiple observations. But how? He reportedly used the midrange (halfway between the lowest and highest values). Even by the 17th century, great thinkers including Johannes Kepler, Tycho Brahe, and Galileo still hadn’t come to a consensus, variously using the midrange, median, sometimes the mean, and sometimes methods that they just made up themselves and didn’t particularly bother to explain (Stahl, 2006).
It was over the course of the 18th century that the mean began to become the standard. By 1777, mathematician and physicist Daniel Bernoulli2 wrote that among astronomers (who “as a class are men of the most scrupulous sagacity”), the mean had become a “universally accepted rule for handling several slightly discrepant observations of the same event” (Bernoulli, 1961, p. 3).3
Why is the mean so valuable for handling discrepant observations? Well, when your measurements of the same thing come out a bit different each time, how can you know which one to trust? The mean, in a sense, allows us to trust no one observation in particular, but rather to put them all together and allow the “errors” to cancel out.
To see what I mean, consider the foot — as in the imperial unit of distance. Things have been measured in feet for a long time, since a foot is a convenient human-scale unit, and usually easy to come by. Just look down. But obviously it’s not very standardized. My foot isn’t necessarily the same length as yours. This can lead to trouble. A “rod” was a common unit of land measurement, generally defined as something like 16 feet. But because of the issue of unstandardized feet, different towns often had different standards for what exactly a rod was, opening the door to property and taxation disputes when administering surveys across regions.
In his surveying manual Geometrei, the sixteenth-century mathematician and general Renaissance man Jakob Köbel offered a solution.

Stand at the door of a church on a Sunday and bid 16 men to stop, tall ones and small ones, as they happen to pass out when the service is finished; then make them put their feet one behind the other, and the length thus obtained shall be a right and lawful rod to measure and survey the land with, and the 16th part of it shall be the right and lawful foot.(Addy, 1925, p. 215)




Figure 3.5: Sixteen men line up their feet toe to heel to establish a surveying rod. Woodcut from Jakob Köbel’s Geometrei, first published in 1535 or 1536. Image from Addy (1925).






This practical procedure illustrates the logic of the mean. Any one foot (as in, the foot at the end of someone’s leg) is a bit different from any other. But if we take a bunch of them and figure out the average, we end up with an idealized foot that can be used as a more standardized and reliable unit of length than any one actual foot.
Note how the mean provides a model of the thing being measured. The sixteenth part of the measured rod — the idealized average “foot” — will not necessarily be the same as any of the individual feet from which it was calculated. The mean represents an ideal, not the actual. This is a powerful and useful thing. We can use the ideal foot without having to deal with all the individual idiosyncratic feet. But if we rely on ideals and neglect reality, we can get into another kind of trouble.
This becomes most obvious when the mean is used to describe and understand people. (Not just their feet.) Belgian astronomer, statistician, and pioneering sociologist Adolphe Quetelet adopted statistical techniques like the average to understand human and social data. In his 1846 book Letters on the Theory of Probabilities, as Applied to the Moral and Political Sciences, Quetelet examined the chest circumference measurements of more than 5,000 Scottish soldiers. He treated each soldier’s distance from the mean like an astronomer treated an observation’s distance from the true position of a star: as error (Gallagher, 2020). The mean represented the “true” soldier; actual soldiers were imperfect variations. Quetelet called this abstraction l’homme moyen, the average man. He saw in l’homme moyen the possibility of the same kind of harmonious proportion in health, beauty, and moral balance that the Pythagoreans found in music. An individual combining all of the average man’s qualities would represent “everything grand, beautiful, and good” and resemble a “type of perfection” (Quetelet, 1835, pp. 274–276).
Quetelet acknowledged, however, that this perfect identity could “scarcely be realized.” No one person can be average in every respect, and statistical findings from the masses should not be mechanically applied to individuals. A doctor should not merely treat every patient as if they were average but rather consider each individually (Quetelet, 1835, pp. 267–269).
The French modernist architect Le Corbusier did not allow any such reservations to constrain his own work. In designing buildings and urban spaces, Corbusier calculated people’s requirements for air, heat, light, and space, turning statistical abstractions and quantitative assumptions into blueprints for reality. Real people, as opposed to statistical aggregates, want their living spaces to do more than satisfy minimum physical requirements. They cook, work, socialize, gossip, relax, and make a place their own. But Le Corbusier brushed this aside: “Each man will live in an ordered relation to the whole.” No need to worry about individual wants, hopes, desires, because “human happiness already exists expressed in terms of numbers, of mathematics, of properly calculated designs” (Scott, 1998, pp. 112–113).
The reason I bring all this up here is to show that the mean is a simple and powerful tool, but we should not let its mathematical elegance lull us into forgetting that we are dealing with a deliberately simplified statistical summary rather than a direct representation of reality.

Calculating the mean
Ok, history lesson over. Let’s talk more about the math. Again, when we want to calculate the mean, all we do is sum the scores and then divide by the number of scores. (Since we’re doing real math here, the mean only works with quantitative data; a mean cannot be computed for categorical data.)
\[  \mu = \frac{\Sigma X}{N}  \tag{3.1}\]
\[  M = \frac{\Sigma X}{n}  \tag{3.2}\]
The \(\Sigma\) symbol tells us to add, and \(X\) represents each score. The other symbols differ depending on whether we’re talking about a sample or a population. For a population (Equation 3.1), we call the mean \(\mu\) and divide by uppercase \(N\), the number of individuals in the population. For a sample (Equation 3.2), we call the mean \(M\) and divide by lowercase \(n\), the number of observations in the sample. (Sometimes statisticians refer to the mean as \(\bar{X}\) (“x bar”). But social scientists generally use this \(\mu\) or \(M\) notation, so, with apologies to real statisticians, that’s what we’re going to use for our purposes.)
Why is this such an elegant and effective statistic? In our historical tour we encountered the idea of measurement errors, as when an astronomer might measure an angle slightly too low today and slightly too high tomorrow. And we also mentioned another kind of variability, as when some soldiers’ chest circumferences are bigger than average and some are smaller than average. Let me now use the more neutral term deviations.
A deviation is the difference between a score and some reference point, keeping track of direction. Here we can think about deviations from the mean. A score \(X\) above the mean has a positive deviation, while a score below it has a negative deviation. We can express the difference as \(X - M\). If we calculate the deviation for every score and then add them up, we always get the same answer: \(\Sigma(X - M) = 0\). This is what is special about the mean. It is the one reference point around which the signed deviations sum to zero.
Here’s a sort of visual, physical way of thinking about the average. Picture the kind of block histogram we mentioned in the previous chapter, with scores as boxes piled up on the x axis categories. And picture the x axis itself as a balance beam, perched on top of a pivot. The mean is the point along the x axis where scores are “balanced,” with the same “weight,” so to speak, on either side. Notice that there are two boxes to the left and three to the right. Balance doesn’t require the same number of boxes on each side: a box farther from the pivot has more leverage than one close to it.






Activity 3.2: The mean as a balance point





Stepped balance-beam demonstration. Five observations balance at their mean of 5. Their signed deviations sum to zero; moving the pivot or adding a new observation tips the beam until the pivot moves to the new mean.




Here’s a small set of scores represented as boxes on a balance beam. For this little dataset, \(\Sigma X = 1+2+6+6+10=25\), so \(M=25/5=5\). That’s where the pivot sits to balance the beam.


We can label each box by its deviation from \(M = 5\): its distance above or below the mean. The scores to the left are 4 and 3 points below the mean. To the right, two scores are 1 point above it and one is 5 points above it.


The lines at the bottom add those deviations end to end. The negative deviations sum to −7 and the positive deviations sum to +7. They balance. This is what it means for the deviations to sum to zero, \(\Sigma (X - M) = 0\).


Suppose we tried to balance the scores at 4 instead. The deviations are now measured from that point, and they no longer cancel out: the negative side sums to −5 while the positive side sums to +10. So the beam is no longer balanced, and it tips over.


Returning the pivot to the mean restores the balance, for this particular set of scores. But what if the scores changed? The mean would have to change too.


Let’s add one more observation at 2 while leaving the pivot at the old mean of 5. The new score adds another negative deviation, so the two sides no longer cancel out and the beam tips again. The mean of the expanded set must have changed.


The six scores sum to 27, so the new mean is \(27/6\), or 4.5. Moving the pivot to that point restores the balance: the negative deviations and positive deviations once again cancel out.


Now try changing the distribution yourself. Drag the red pivot to test another balance point. Click an empty spot to add a box, or click an existing box to remove it.




How does this balancing act work? \(\Sigma X\) lumps all the observed scores into one total. Dividing that total by \(n\) shares it equally among the \(n\) observations. Imagine a bunch of people holding identical buckets containing different amounts of water (\(X\)). Some people’s buckets are almost filled to the brim, some people’s are almost empty. We have them all dump their water into one big tank (\(\Sigma X\)), and then share it back out equally (divide by \(n\)). Now everyone has exactly the same amount in their bucket (the average amount, \(M\)).
Put mathematically, \(M=\frac{\Sigma X}{n}\) rearranges to \(nM=\Sigma X\). If we replace every observed score with the mean (\(nM\)) we get the same total (\(\Sigma X\)). The extra water in some buckets is exactly matched by the shortfall in others; the deviations balance.

title: 3  Central Tendency
text:
Comparing the three measures
Now we’ve explored the ins and outs of three measures of central tendency: the mode describes the most frequent score (or scores); the median orders the observations and divides them in half; the mean balances their values. When we can compute all three measures for a quantitative distribution, we might find that they pretty much agree, or that they diverge.
To see why, let’s start with an extreme example. Suppose we stand on a street corner and ask the people passing by their incomes. For some reason, they agree to tell us, and we list the first seven answers below.

🙂 $30,000
🙂 $40,000
🙂 $45,000
🙂 $50,000
🙂 $55,000
🙂 $60,000
🙂 $70,000

We can locate the median right in the middle of the ordered incomes at $50,000. We can also calculate the mean by adding up all the values and dividing by 7. At this point, we’d find that it’s the same as the median, $50,000.
But the next person who walks by happens to be real estate tycoon Mr. Monopoly, with an annual income of a billion dollars.4 Now our data look like this:

🙂 $30,000
🙂 $40,000
🙂 $45,000
🙂 $50,000
🙂 $55,000
🙂 $60,000
🙂 $70,000
🤑 $1,000,000,000

If we recalculate the median, we find that it hasn’t budged much. It’s $52,500, halfway between the fourth and fifth values. As we’ve seen, the median depends primarily on position. Four incomes fall on either side of it. It doesn’t matter too much what the values at either end of the distribution are. Once Mr. Monopoly is at the upper end, his income could be one hundred thousand dollars or ten billion dollars; the median would be the same either way.
If we recalculate the mean, however, we find that it shoots up to around $125 million. The reason is that the mean balances all the deviations, and an extreme deviation requires the mean to move to accommodate it. So now exactly what Mr. Monopoly’s income is matters, and the farther it is from all the other observations, the more it pulls the mean in that direction. (To see this in action, go back to the mean balance beam and add a box close to the mean, then remove it and add one far away. Which one moves the balance point more?)
Obviously, this is an intentionally contrived example, but this is a genuine issue for researchers who are interested in income distributions. U.S. household income forms a positively skewed distribution. A relatively small number of households have extremely high incomes, while most have much lower incomes. For census data from 2024, the median and mean diverge by almost $40,000 (see Figure 3.6). Our choice of which to report or focus on can give quite a different impression of the “typical” household’s income.



Figure 3.6: Distribution of U.S. household income in 2024, with mean and median markers. Histogram bars represent $5,000 bins, except for the final striped bar which combines all households with incomes of $200,000 or more (16% of households). Data source: U.S. Census Bureau.




Histogram of U.S. household income with mean and median markers.





To take another example, we pointed out the bimodality of the tone-identification data from earlier in the chapter. But that distribution is also a bit skewed. The two peaks are not exactly the same height; the whole distribution is a bit more clustered at the lower-performing end, and skewed a bit by the smaller number of high performers. The median remains near the upper edge of the larger, lower-performing cluster, while the mean is pulled farther toward the space between the two peaks. Arguably, for these data, any one measure of central tendency on its own doesn’t tell the complete story of the distribution’s shape.



Figure 3.7: Distribution of tone-identification performance with the median and mean estimated from the grouped data. Recreated from Chubb et al. (2013), Figure 6.




Histogram of proportion correct for 275 listeners, with an estimated median of 0.62 and mean of 0.67. The distribution has peaks near chance performance at 0.5 and near perfect performance at 1.0.





Stepping back from real data and looking instead at generic distribution curves, we can watch how those three kinds of center respond to changes in normality, skew, and bimodality.






Activity 3.3: Watch the center change





A distribution changes from one symmetrical peak, where the mode, median, and mean coincide, through positive skew, where the mean lies farthest into the tail, back through symmetry into negative skew, and finally into two symmetrical peaks, where the mean and median lie in the valley between the modes.




We begin with a normal distribution, symmetrical and with one peak. The mode is in the middle, where the highest frequency is observed. The median divides the distribution into two halves, right in the middle. And the mean is the balance point, also right in the middle. In this case, all three measures point to the same place because the distribution is symmetrical and unimodal.


Now we can start to make the distribution asymmetrical. Here we see positive skew: a tail begins to grow toward the higher end of the scale. The three markers begin to differ because their definitions respond to different features of the distribution.


The more the distribution is skewed, the more the measures diverge. The mode stays at the peak, where scores are most concentrated. The median moves to the right to keep half the distribution on either side. The mean moves farthest toward the tail: values far from the old balance point have more leverage, as they did in the income example.


With negative skew, the pattern is the opposite. The mode is the highest of the three values, because that’s where the peak is. The median is lower, keeping half of the distribution above and below. And the mean is lowest.


If the distribution is bimodal, we label both modal peaks. Since the distribution is symmetrical again, the median and mean align in the middle. But that middle is a valley containing relatively few observations. The modal peaks on either side show where scores are actually concentrated.

title: 3  Central Tendency
text:
Summary
Each measure of central tendency we’ve covered has pros and cons. The mode works with any variable type and can reveal more than one peak, but it can be less useful when the data is widely scattered and no single value is particularly representative. The median divides ordered data at the 50th percentile and is less influenced by outliers than the mean, but it ignores how far observations fall from that middle. The mean balances all the numeric values, making it especially useful for the analyses we’ll meet later, but it requires quantitative data and can be shifted more substantially by outliers. For reasonably symmetrical, single-peaked quantitative data, all three measures of central tendency often point to roughly the same place. When they don’t, the difference tells us something about the shape of the distribution.
Moving forward, the mean will be our measure of choice, because we’ll most often be dealing with quantitative data where the mean can acknowledge every data point. And as we’ll see, part of its value to us is in those deviations which it balances. We won’t overlook them; in fact, they’ll be central to much of what we end up doing. The mean offers us a model of a world in which everyone is identical; we could replace Köbel’s sixteen churchgoers with sixteen stand-ins, identical mannequins whose feet were all exactly average, and end up with the same answer for the length of the rod. That’s useful. But if shoes only came in one size, “average,” a lot of people would be left uncomfortable. In the real world, things do deviate from the mean. This kind of variability is worth quantifying, which is what we’ll turn to in the next chapter.

title: 4  Variability
text:
What is variability?
In the previous chapter we talked about measures of central tendency. But there is another crucial characteristic of distributions that we need to know in addition to the center: how widely scattered or closely clustered scores are around it. That’s what we mean by variability. We’ll start with the range, then build up the standard deviation from deviations, sums of squares, and variance. Along the way we’ll meet another important concept: degrees of freedom.
To start with, let’s consider a few small sets of scores. Imagine you check the reviews of three movies you’re thinking about watching, scored from 0 to 10.
Using the tools we explored in the previous chapter, we find that the median and mean are 5 for all three movies. The mode is also 5 for the first two. The Polarizing Express has two modes, 0 and 10, which already gives us a clue that something different is going on. But none of these measures quantifies just how closely the ratings cluster around the center. If we plot the ratings as block histograms, we can see what they’re leaving out.
The ratings for Fine, Actually do not vary at all: every reviewer so far gave it a 5. Most of the ratings for The Good, the Bad and the Okay cluster in the middle, aside from the two extremes. The ratings for The Polarizing Express sit much farther towards the extremes, with none in the middle of the scale at all. So Fine, Actually has no variability, The Polarizing Express has relatively high variability, and The Good, the Bad and the Okay sits somewhere in between. The mean gives us the same prediction for all three, but their variability tells us how far individual ratings tend to depart from it.
How do we quantify that difference? Like measures of central tendency, measures of variability use a single number to summarize a more complex dataset. But this time we’re describing spread rather than center. Greater variability means scores are more widely dispersed, so the center by itself tells us less about what any individual score is likely to look like. And, as with central tendency, there is more than one way to quantify it.

title: 4  Variability
text:
The range
Remember Hipparchus? I mentioned him in Chapter 3 as an early astronomical pioneer, gazing at the heavens, taking measurements, and realizing that his data were not always perfectly consistent. His solution (according to later sources; his own original work is mostly lost) was to take the midrange: the halfway point between the lowest and highest observations (Stahl, 2006).
The utility of this to the early astronomers was to smooth over the discrepant measurements; once the midrange was calculated it could be taken as providing a reliable answer, and the extremes could be largely ignored. But those two values also offer a simple and intuitive way of quantifying variability: the range, calculated by subtracting the minimum score from the maximum.
Here are those movie ratings from before:

Fine, Actually: 5, 5, 5, 5, 5, 5
Range: \(5 - 5 = 0\)
The Good, the Bad and the Okay: 0, 4, 5, 5, 6, 10
Range: \(10 - 0 = 10\)
The Polarizing Express: 0, 0, 1, 9, 10, 10
Range: \(10 - 0 = 10\)

The range captures one important difference: it is zero for Fine, Actually because its ratings don’t vary. But it gives us the same answer for The Good, the Bad and the Okay and The Polarizing Express. There’s nothing wrong about that. The range is telling us precisely what it is designed to, but it misses the obvious difference between how the ratings are distributed between the extremes.
This is the main limitation of the range as a measure of variability: it does not consider all the observations. Only the two extremes contribute to its value. As a result, it is not affected by how observations are distributed between them. This characteristic also makes it highly susceptible to outliers. One unusual observation can drastically change the range. It also tends to grow with sample size, simply because larger samples have more opportunities to include extreme values.
That’s not to say looking at the range isn’t useful for some purposes. Researchers often begin by checking the minimum, maximum, and range to get a quick sense of the values in their data. Sometimes you just don’t know what to expect, so it’s helpful to see the extremes and how far apart they are. It can also reveal a problem. Suppose we write a new extraversion item that allows responses numbered one to five. A range of three might make us wonder why part of the response scale went unused. Maybe asking people “Are you the world’s most extraverted person?” was a bit too much and restricted the range of responses. A range of ten, on the other hand, tells us to check for misrecorded values.
Useful as the range is, we also want a measure of variability that considers every observation, not just the two extremes. For that, we need a more mathematically sophisticated measure.

title: 4  Variability
text:
Deviations
In Chapter 3 we introduced deviations: the differences between each score and the mean. The mean is the point at which those deviations balance, but the deviations themselves also give us a way to quantify how far the scores spread around it.
Astronomers realized this too. Deviations offered a way to quantify the imprecision of their instruments or observations. For statisticians applying the same ideas to human measurements, they captured a different kind of variation. In Quetelet’s measurements of soldiers’ chests, a deviation did not necessarily indicate a mistake of the measuring tape; it described how one person’s body differed from another’s. In either case, if we think of the mean as a prediction, a deviation is the prediction error: how far, and in which direction, the actual score fell from it.
The next step was to find a way to summarize those deviations in a single number. Should be easy, no? If we want a “standard deviation,” meaning a typical deviation from the mean, an obvious solution would be to calculate the average of all the deviations. Before we go any further, think through what answer that calculation would give us.



Why can’t we simply average the raw deviations from the mean?Show hintShow answerCheck your workClearAnswerThe mean is the balance point of the distribution, so the negative
deviations below it and the positive deviations above it balance each
other out. The signed deviations therefore always add up to zero. Their
average would be zero too, no matter how much the scores varied.


Quiz 4.2



So we need a different strategy. One option would be to take the absolute value of every deviation, dropping the minus sign from the negative ones, and then find the mean absolute deviation. But the strategy we’re going to focus on is squaring each deviation. Squaring solves the problem by turning the negative deviations into positive values, so they no longer cancel out the deviations above the mean when we sum them.1
Having squared the deviations, we can continue with one connected chain of calculations. Add the squared deviations to get \(SS\), the sum of squared deviations (or “sum of squares” for short). Divide \(SS\) by the number of observations to get the population variance, the mean squared deviation. Then take its square root to get the standard deviation. The square root returns us to the original units, so we can interpret the standard deviation as a typical deviation from the mean.2

title: 4  Variability
text:
Variability equations for populations
To complicate life slightly, populations and samples use slightly different calculations. We’ll start with a population and return to samples shortly.
The table puts the steps into mathematical notation. Population variance is represented by lowercase sigma squared (\(\sigma^2\)), and population standard deviation by lowercase sigma (\(\sigma\)).



Table 4.1: Summary and notation for calculating population variance and standard deviation.










Step
Calculation




1. Find the deviation for each score
\(X - \mu\)


2. Square the deviations
\((X - \mu)^2\)


3. Sum the squared deviations
\(SS = \Sigma(X - \mu)^2\)


4. Calculate variance (mean squared deviation)
\(\sigma^2 = \frac{SS}{N}\)


5. Calculate standard deviation (root-mean-square deviation)
\(\sigma = \sqrt{\sigma^2}\)







Equations in hand, let’s return to the two movies whose ratings had the same range. For now, we’ll treat each complete set of ratings as its own population. We’ll work through The Good, the Bad and the Okay together, following that sequence of five steps; then you can try the same procedure for The Polarizing Express.






Activity 4.1: Calculate variability





Interactive table calculating deviations, sum of squares, variance, and standard deviation for the ratings of The Good, the Bad and the Okay.




When I’m doing these calculations by hand, I find it easiest to put the scores in the first column of a table, labeled \(X\). We’ll add to this table as we go along. So here are the original ratings for The Good, the Bad and the Okay.


First find the population mean. The ratings add to 30, and there are six of them, so \(\mu = 30/6 = 5\). This will be the reference point for every deviation in the next column.


Now I add a column for the deviations. Subtract the mean from each score: \(X-\mu\). The deviations are \(-5, -1, 0, 0, 1,\) and \(5\). The signs tell us which side of the mean the scores fall on, while the sizes tell us how far away they are. If you simply add up these six values, you get an answer of zero.


Next I add a column for the squared deviations. This gives us \(25, 1, 0, 0, 1,\) and \(25\). Squaring makes every value nonnegative, so when we add them up in the next step we won’t get zero.


Now we add up all the squared deviations to get the sum of squares: \(SS = 25+1+0+0+1+25 = 52\).


Next divide \(SS\) by the population size, \(N\), to get the variance: \(\sigma^2 = 52/6 = 8.67\). Because we’ve squared the deviations, variance is measured in squared rating points. That makes it useful mathematically, but not especially intuitive on the scale of the original scores.


Finally, take the square root of the variance: \(\sigma = \sqrt{8.67} = 2.94\). This returns us to the original units, so we can say that a typical deviation from the mean rating for The Good, the Bad and the Okay is around three points.

6\), and take the square root.Answer4.69ExplanationThe mean rating is \(\mu = 5\). Here
is the whole calculation:


Filled variability table for the ratings of The Polarizing Express,
showing deviations, squared deviations, SS = 132, population variance =
22, and population standard deviation = 4.69.


Taking the square root of 22 gives a standard deviation of 4.69. This
is larger than the 2.94 for The Good, the Bad and the Okay, capturing
the greater spread that the range missed.


Quiz 4.3




The importance of sums of squares
Allow me for a moment to impress upon you the importance of squares. \(SS\) is not just an intermediate answer that we can forget about as soon as we’ve found the standard deviation. Later in this book we’ll find ourselves splitting variability into different sources, each with its own sum of squares. By the time we finish ANOVA and regression near the end of the semester, I like to joke with my students that the whole course has been nothing but squares all the way down.
The tables above followed the definitional formula for \(SS\): find each deviation, square it, and add the squared deviations.
\[
SS = \Sigma(X - \mu)^2
\]
There is an algebraically equivalent shortcut called the computational formula:
\[
SS = \Sigma X^2 - \frac{(\Sigma X)^2}{N}
\]
Order of operations is important here. For the first term, \(\Sigma X^2\), square every score and sum the results. Then subtract the correction term: the sum of the scores squared, divided by the number of scores. For The Good, the Bad and the Okay, \(\Sigma X=30\) and \(\Sigma X^2=202\), so:
\[
SS = 202 - \frac{30^2}{6} = 202 - 150 = 52
\]
That is the same answer we found in Activity 4.1 following the definitional approach. The shortcut likewise gives \(SS=132\) for The Polarizing Express, so the rest of both calculations remains unchanged.
We’ll stick with the definitional approach for now, but tuck this computational arrangement in the back of your mind; it will become our preferred method when we get to the ANOVA section of the book.

title: 4  Variability
text:
Sample variability and bias
So far we’ve treated the movie ratings as populations. I mentioned that we have to do things a little differently for samples. Don’t worry, the difference in the math is tiny, but the reason for it is important.
Like I mentioned in Chapter 1, there’s overlap between descriptive and inferential statistics. Here, we want to know our sample’s variance, but not because we especially care about the sample itself. Rather, we want to use it as an estimate of the population variance. The trouble is that if we used precisely the calculation above, dividing \(SS\) by \(n\), the estimate would be biased.
Bias does not mean that any one sample estimate is wrong: a sample’s variance can over- or underestimate its population variance. Bias is a long-run tendency. An unbiased estimator is sometimes too high, sometimes too low, but those errors balance out in the long run. A biased estimator systematically leans in one direction. If we repeatedly took samples and calculated variance by dividing \(SS\) by \(n\), the average of all the estimates would be less than the actual population variance; it would underestimate the true value.
The bias comes from using the sample mean, \(M\), in place of the unknown \(\mu\). Each sample’s \(M\) is fitted to the scores in that particular sample, designed to minimize their sum of squared deviations. As a result, the sum of squared deviations around \(M\) can never be larger than the sum of squared deviations of those same scores around \(\mu\), and will be smaller unless \(M = \mu\).






Activity 4.2: The moving center





Interactive sampling diagram comparing the same sample's deviations around its fitted mean and the fixed population mean.




Here we have a happy little population, a symmetrical mound of colorful dots. It has a fixed mean, \(\mu\), and standard deviation, \(\sigma\). The length of the black line underneath shows \(\mu \pm \sigma\). We’ll use that fixed span as our reference length, so in this picture \(\sigma =\) ....


Now we draw a sample of ... dots from the population. We want to compute the variability of the sample, but how?


Because this is a simulation, we know \(\mu\). So we can calculate the sample’s squared deviations from \(\mu\), divide by \(n\) to get variance, and take the square root to get SD. The dashed blue line shows the answer relative to the population SD: .... This is the SD we would get using the fixed population mean.


But usually we can’t do that: we don’t know \(\mu\)! So instead we find the sample mean, \(M\), and calculate the squared deviations around it. The solid red line shows that answer, ..., centered on \(M\) because that’s how we calculated it.


Now that we’ve calculated it, let’s slide the red span over so all three SD lines are centered on \(\mu\) and we can compare them. The red span fits inside the dashed blue one. Computing the sample’s SD around \(M\) rather than \(\mu\) gave a smaller answer.


A new sample gives us a different \(M\), and different standard deviations computed around \(\mu\) or \(M\) (the actual population \(\sigma\) is fixed and doesn’t change). Here the red sample SD is larger than the actual population \(\sigma\). An individual sample can still overestimate variability. But the red \(M\)-based span is still no wider than the dashed \(\mu\)-based span.


For every new sample, the red line will be narrower than the blue one (or they might be the same if the sample mean \(M\) happens to be equal to \(\mu\)).


Keep clicking to take as many new samples as you like. Both computed standard deviations will change, and either can land above or below the population SD. But the \(M\)-based answer can never be larger than the \(\mu\)-based answer for the same observations, because it is always fitted to the new sample mean—a moving target. That built-in shrinkage is what creates the long-run bias.

title: 4  Variability
text:
Variability equations for samples
So now we know what the problem is, here’s the solution: divide \(SS\) by \(n - 1\) rather than \(n\). If only all of life’s problems were so easily solved.
The adjusted denominator makes sample variance, \(s^2\), an unbiased estimator of population variance. Taking its square root gives the usual sample standard deviation, \(s\), often labeled \(SD\) when results are reported in psychology.3
Here is the table of steps and equations again, with a new column applying them to samples. There are differences in notation—the Greek symbols \(\mu\) and \(\sigma\) and uppercase \(N\) for populations; \(M\), \(s\), and \(n\) for samples. But aside from the different denominator in step 4, the process is the same.



Table 4.2: Summary and notation for calculating population and sample variance and standard deviation.











Step
Population
Sample




1. Find the deviation for each score
\(X - \mu\)
\(X - M\)


2. Square the deviations
\((X - \mu)^2\)
\((X - M)^2\)


3. Sum the squared deviations
\(SS = \Sigma(X - \mu)^2\)
\(SS = \Sigma(X - M)^2\)


4. Calculate variance
\(\sigma^2 = \frac{SS}{N}\)
\(s^2 = \frac{SS}{df} = \frac{SS}{n - 1}\)


5. Calculate standard deviation
\(\sigma = \sqrt{\sigma^2}\)
\(s = \sqrt{s^2}\)

title: 4  Variability
text:
Degrees of freedom
Well, it’s not quite as simple as I made it sound there. To fully understand the issue and why this solution works, we need to know about \(df\), which I snuck into Table 4.2. That refers to degrees of freedom. For ordinary sample variance, \(df = n - 1\). More generally, a variance is a sum of squares divided by the degrees of freedom associated with it, and \(df\) is not always \(n - 1\) as it is in this case. Later, in ANOVA, we’ll split variability into several sums of squares, each with its own \(df\).
So why does the correction here use exactly \(n - 1\)? It is a result of the constraint imposed by calculating deviations from the sample mean. Doing so costs us one degree of freedom.
To illustrate, suppose I put three playing cards face down in front of you and tell you that the mean of their values is \(M=5\). I point to the first card and ask you what number you think it is. There is no way for you to know, of course, so you shrug and I show you that it is a three. I point to the second card. You still can’t know what it is; I turn it over and reveal a five. Now I point to the last card. Can you tell me its number? You jump up and exclaim, “eureka!” Given the mean and the other two values, there’s only one thing this last one can be: it has to be seven.

We could shuffle the same three cards and repeat the process; the order the cards are turned over in doesn’t matter. And we could have more than three cards. Whatever the last card is, we’ll always be able to determine its value without turning it over. Fixing the mean imposes a constraint. Only two of the three values are free to vary. The same applies to deviations around the sample mean: once \(M\) has been fitted, the deviations have to sum to zero. Any \(n - 1\) deviations can vary, but their values determine the last one. So sample variance has \(df = n - 1\) degrees of freedom.
If \(\mu\) were already known and we measured the sample’s deviations around that fixed population center, they would not be constrained to sum to zero and we would not lose a degree of freedom by fitting \(M\). (Later we’ll meet calculations that fit more means and therefore have different degrees of freedom.)

title: 4  Variability
text:
Sampling error and statistical bias
One last thing. Now that we know about statistical bias, you might be worried about other statistics being biased. What about the mean? We spent most of Chapter 3 talking about it, but never mentioned bias. It shouldn’t get off the hook, right? We ought to check if it is biased or unbiased. And turning back to variance, Activity 4.2 illustrated the cause of its bias, but it didn’t show the correction. And it only showed one sample at a time. Like we said, bias operates in the aggregate.
It would help to be more precise about the term error. An estimate can differ from the true parameter for different reasons. Sometimes it is thrown off by a genuine mistake or a bad design choice. But even under ideal circumstances, a statistic calculated from one sample will usually not be exactly equal to the corresponding population parameter. This kind of naturally-occuring discrepancy, inherent to the process of sampling from a population, is sampling error.
Bias, by contrast, is a long-run property. Across repeated samples, do a statistic’s errors balance around zero, or do they systematically lean in one direction? Dividing \(SS\) by \(n - 1\) doesn’t make every variance estimate perfectly accurate; sampling error means each individual estimate can still be too high or too low. But it makes the overestimates and underestimates balance out in the long run. To see the difference between sampling error and bias, we need to look at many estimates.






Activity 4.3: Tracking bias across repeated samples





Interactive charts tracking mean and variance estimates across repeated samples.




Here’s our happy little population again. We’ll use it to track long-run bias in a couple of statistics. First we’ll check whether the sample mean, \(M\), is biased or unbiased. Then we’ll compare the two calculations we learned, dividing \(SS\) either by \(n\) or by \(n - 1\) to compute sample variance.


Here’s our first sample. Its mean is a little below the true population mean. But again, bias is not about any one sample over- or underestimating its parameter. We need to track this across a bunch of samples.


The population will stay the same while we draw sample after sample, so let’s shift it out of the way and collect the individual sample means on the timeline below. Each square’s vertical position is that sample’s estimation error, \(M-\mu\): below zero is an underestimate and above zero is an overestimate. The first sample’s mean is a little below the population mean, so it lands just below zero.


Now we draw nine more samples, one at a time. The ten squares are the ten sample means we’ve seen so far. We’ve got some below zero, some above it, and some very close to zero, where the sample mean was very close to \(\mu\).


This second tracker summarizes the first. After each new sample, it averages all the errors collected so far. So the end of the line is the average of all ten means’ errors so far. Bias is the long-run position of this average, not the fact that individual estimates scatter around. But ten is not much of a long run. Let’s make room for a lot more.


Now we have space for 1,000 means. Nothing else has changed: these are still the same ten sample means, and the cumulative line still summarizes only those ten errors. When you click next, watch as a whole lot more samples are taken, their means added to the first tracker, and the cumulative average error updates in the second tracker.


Once all 1,000 sample means have been collected, the average error is very close to zero. The individual errors on the top tracker scatter evenly above and below the 0 line. The cumulative average error line—the running average of all those means—has meandered up and down, but it has no long-run tendency to stay above or below zero. The sample mean is an unbiased estimator of the population mean.


Now let’s estimate population variance by dividing \(SS\) by \(n\), without the correction. The black span is the true population variance; the red span is this sample’s estimate. I’ve lined them up at the same center so we can compare their lengths directly (though the sample variance uses deviations from the sample mean). One estimate can miss high or low, so it still cannot establish bias. This one, even though it uses the wrong denominator, happens to be almost exactly right, so sits at 0 on the error tracker.


Now let’s repeat that calculation across 1,000 samples. The individual red estimates scatter above and below zero, but their cumulative average settles below it. The errors do not balance out: dividing by \(n\) systematically underestimates population variance.


We can go back through those same 1,000 samples and recompute the variance using the corrected \(n - 1\) denominator. We’ll start again with the first sample. Above the dots, the green corrected span replaces the red uncorrected one. In the trackers, we’ll keep all the red results where they are and begin adding the green results. The samples are identical. With the new, correct denominator, this variance happens to overestimate the true value. But again, one sample can’t establish bias.


Now we replay the same 1,000 samples. The green corrected squares are added on top of the existing red estimates, and the green cumulative line gets drawn as we average those new values together. Dividing by \(n - 1\) inflates each estimate just enough, on average, for the green line to settle around zero while the red line remained below it. The individual estimates still scatter around the true value due to sampling error, but the correction eliminates the long-run bias.




So phew, the mean is an unbiased estimator of the population mean.4 Sampling error is not an error in the colloquial sense of something we did wrong and could have avoided. It is a natural consequence of taking a sample. Sometimes the error is in the direction of overestimating the mean, sometimes underestimating it, but in the long run those random errors balance out and the mean is unbiased.
Sample variance can be an unbiased estimator of population variance too, as long as we divide \(SS\) by \(df\) (\(n - 1\) in this situation). Dividing by \(n\) does not stop the estimates from varying randomly; it shifts their long-run center downward. Individual estimates can still be too high or too low, but their errors average below zero, as we saw in the cumulative average of the 1,000 variance estimates calculated with the uncorrected denominator. The green line, where we divided by \(n - 1\), fluctuated along the way but made its way close to zero in the long run.

title: 4  Variability
text:
The mean absolute deviation from the mean is a perfectly legitimate measure of variability, and it is less affected by extreme scores because it does not square their distances. But squaring has some other mathematical properties that will become useful when we get around to partitioning variance later in the book. As usual, statistics don’t invent and apply themselves: we still have to think about which measure makes the most sense for what we’re trying to do.↩︎
More precisely, the population standard deviation is the root-mean-square deviation: we square the deviations, find their mean, and take the square root. “Typical deviation” is a useful interpretation, but it isn’t the literal arithmetic mean of the raw deviations or their absolute values. I don’t hear social scientists use the term “root-mean-square deviation” very often, so I’m just going to follow the convention of calling it the standard deviation.↩︎
Strictly speaking, taking the square root introduces a small downward bias, especially with very small samples. But \(s\) is much less biased than an uncorrected standard deviation based on \(SS/n\).↩︎
More precisely, the sample mean is an unbiased estimator of the population mean under the random-sampling setup used here. Bias can be introduced in other ways, but that’s an issue for another time.↩︎

title: 5  \(z\)-Scores
text:
Comparing scores
In the last two chapters, we’ve covered central tendency, particularly the mean, and variability, particularly focusing on standard deviation. Now we’ll see how we can combine these two statistics into a new concept: the \(z\)-score. We’ll talk about what \(z\)-scores are for and how we calculate them. Then we’ll talk more about describing distributions, particularly what we mean by standardized distributions. And lastly, we’ll see how we can begin to think about making probabilistic inferences using this new tool.
To see why this is such a useful way of describing scores, suppose we have created two math tests and given them to a few people already. One test consists of a handful of fairly simple sums:
The second test is more difficult:
We’re curious how long it takes people to complete each test, and whether times for the two tests are related. If somebody is quick on one test are they also quick on the other? Or does performance on one not translate to the other?
Now suppose you take each of the tests, and we record how long they each take you. You’re done with the first in 8 seconds, while the second takes you 70 seconds.
You sense a problem, right? I’m asking you to compare performances, but the tests are pretty different. There’s no reason to expect that your time would be similar; indeed we should expect quite different times. So should we just give up trying to compare at all? Not so fast! We have more information. Remember, we already gave some people these tests. So let’s say we know that on average it takes people 10 seconds to complete the first test and 100 seconds to complete the second.
Faster than average on both tests. Not too shabby. But wait a minute. Can we be more precise? What if we have one more piece of information: the standard deviation. For the easy test the standard deviation is 1 second; for the hard test it is 15 seconds.
Did you spot the common theme? On each test, you were 2 standard deviations below the mean. So although 8 seconds and 70 seconds are very different times, and they fall a different number of seconds below their respective means, they occupy the same relative position in their respective distributions. The mean and standard deviation together provide context for the raw scores, giving us a common ruler with which to compare them.1

standard-deviation units.


The \(z\)-score
This is the approach to comparing scores described in 1912 by the psychologist R. S. Woodworth of Columbia University. Woodworth didn’t claim to have invented the idea: “Such a method exists, and is certainly familiar to statisticians,” he wrote; “but it seems to be overlooked in many cases where it would prove of value” (Woodworth, 1912).
Woodworth noted that it was common practice to switch from quantitative data to qualitative statements: “to say, for example, that an individual who has done very well in the first test, well in the second, but rather poorly on the third, has on the whole, therefore, done rather well.” Maybe you’ve taken an approach like this if, say, you like most of a director’s films, except for one that you thought was just okay and another that you hated. You’d probably say that you generally like the director’s movies overall: a useful summary, but lacking precision. More numerical approaches, such as counting the tests on which someone performed above average or averaging their ranks, still threw away information. “What is needed,” Woodworth wrote, “is a method of combining results which shall preserve all the refinement of the original measurements.”
Woodworth didn’t give the resulting number a specific name or symbol, and didn’t formalize it as an equation. Here is his description:

Let the average in each case be counted as \(0\), i. e., let the individual’s standing be expressed as a deviation above or below the average; and further, let the measure of variability be taken as the unit deviation, and all deviations be expressed as fractions or multiples of this unit.2

Eventually the term \(z\)-score was attached to this approach. We can represent the population \(z\)-score mathematically: \[z = \frac{X - \mu}{\sigma} \tag{5.1}\]
\(X\) refers to a score, \(\mu\) to the population mean, and \(\sigma\) to the population standard deviation.
If we’re dealing with a sample rather than a population, the calculation is the same but we use the corresponding sample statistics:
\[z = \frac{X - M}{s} \tag{5.2}\]
Here \(M\) is the sample mean and \(s\) is the sample standard deviation.
The numerator in either equation should look familiar: it’s a deviation score, like we’ve encountered in the previous couple of chapters. Dividing a deviation score by the standard deviation expresses that deviation in standard-deviation units. The sign tells us which side of the mean the score falls on. A positive \(z\)-score is above the mean and a negative \(z\)-score is below it. (That doesn’t necessarily mean good or bad: in our example, a negative \(z\)-score means a faster completion time.) The absolute magnitude of the \(z\)-score, written \(|z|\), tells us how many standard deviations the score is from the mean. So if \(z = 0\), the score is exactly equal to the mean. As \(|z|\) increases, the score is farther from the mean.

title: 5  \(z\)-Scores
text:
Computing \(z\)-scores
Let’s look at this visually. Figure 5.1 shows a histogram of completion times for a sample of 30 people who took the easy math test. Remember, for this distribution \(M = 10\) seconds, and the standard deviation is \(s = 1\) second. The dashed line marks your time of 8 seconds, down near the lower end of the distribution.



Figure 5.1: Histogram of completion times on the easy math test for a sample of 30 people. The sample mean is 10 seconds and the sample standard deviation is 1 second; a vertical line marks a time of 8 seconds.




Histogram of completion times for a sample of 30 earlier test takers on the easy math test. The sample mean is 10 seconds and the sample standard deviation is 1 second; a vertical line marks a time of 8 seconds.





Putting those values into the sample equation gives us: \[z = \frac{8 - 10}{1} = \frac{-2}{1} = -2\]
For the hard test, the mean was 100 seconds, the standard deviation was 15 seconds, and your time was 70 seconds. The histogram below marks that original time.



Figure 5.2: Histogram of completion times on the hard math test for a sample of 30 people. The sample mean is 100 seconds and the sample standard deviation is 15 seconds; a vertical line marks a time of 70 seconds.




Histogram of completion times for a sample of 30 earlier test takers on the hard math test. The sample mean is 100 seconds and the sample standard deviation is 15 seconds; a vertical line marks a time of 70 seconds.


\[z = \frac{70 - 100}{15} = \frac{-30}{15} = -2\]



Calculating z-scoresAnother person completes the hard test in 115 seconds. Using the
sample mean of 100 seconds and standard deviation of 15 seconds, what is
the \(z\)-score?Show hintShow answerCheck your workClearAnswer1Explanation\(z = (115 - 100) / 15 = 1\). This
time is one standard deviation above the mean, so it is slower than
average.

Converting back to raw scores
We can also work in the other direction, from a \(z\)-score back to a raw score, if we have the mean and standard deviation. For a sample, if \(z = \frac{X - M}{s}\), then
\[X = M + z \times s \tag{5.3}\]
Here’s what that looks like if we want to work backwards from the two \(z\)-scores to the original completion times.
\[
\begin{align}
\text{Easy test:} \quad X & = M + zs = 10 + (-2) \times 1 = 8 \\
\text{Hard test:} \quad X & = M + zs = 100 + (-2) \times 15 = 70
\end{align}
\]

title: 5  \(z\)-Scores
text:
Standardized distributions
So far, we’ve converted a couple of individual observations into \(z\)-scores. But what if we converted a whole distribution? The result would be a standardized distribution.
A useful way to picture this is as adding a new ruler underneath the distribution. The shape of the distribution doesn’t change; the scores keep the same order and relative positions, but the numbers attached to those positions change.
Here are the two math test distributions again, this time with \(z\)-score rulers underneath their original scales. The original rulers show completion times in seconds, while the new rulers show the corresponding standardized positions. This makes it even clearer how your two times of 8 seconds and 70 seconds occupy the same relative position in their respective distributions. We could compare any \(z\)-score position between the two distributions. Say we wanted to know how many seconds correspond to \(z = 2\)—two standard deviations above the mean—on each test, rather than \(z = -2\). The rulers make that easy to see: it would be 12 seconds on the easy test and 130 seconds on the hard test.



Figure 5.3: Both math test distributions, with a new ‘ruler’ beneath the original x-axis, showing the corresponding \(z\)-scores. The mean, corresponding to \(z = 0\), is marked with a dashed line, as are \(z = -1\) and \(z = 1\), the positions one standard deviation above and below the mean.





Histogram of easy-test completion times with aligned raw-score and z-score rulers; 8 seconds aligns with z = -2.




Histogram of hard-test completion times with aligned raw-score and z-score rulers; 70 seconds aligns with z = -2.







Other standard-score scales
A distribution of \(z\)-scores always has a mean of zero and standard deviation of one, because of how the \(z\)-score formula works. That is a useful standardization, but sometimes it’s not exactly what we want to deal with. So once we’ve converted scores to \(z\)-scores, we can then rescale them to use a more convenient mean and standard deviation, if we want to. These are usually called transformed standard scores.
You’ll already be familiar with some transformed scales like this. SAT section scores were designed to have a mean of 500 and a standard deviation of approximately 100 in a specified reference cohort. (That doesn’t mean every later group of test takers will have exactly those values; see College Board (2017)). Many IQ tests transform scores to use a mean of 100 and a standard deviation of 15. Those values are arbitrary; we could perfectly well just use \(z\)-scores for the job. But imagine telling someone you scored \(z = -0.32\) on the SATs or that your IQ is 1.03. It wouldn’t be wrong to give those measurements as \(z\)-scores, but since they usually entail decimals, negative values, and a relatively small numeric range, they are just a bit finicky and unintuitive. Transforming the means and standard deviations lets us deal mostly in positive whole numbers, which can be a bit easier to talk about.
The procedure to take a standardized distribution of \(z\)-scores and transform it to a new scale, with whatever mean and standard deviation your heart desires, is simple. After standardizing the original scores, so that the mean becomes \(0\) and the standard deviation becomes \(1\), we can then multiply those \(z\)-scores to set a new standard deviation, then add a constant to set a new mean. The tutorial below follows one score from its original scale to the \(z\) scale, then to simplified IQ- and SAT-style reporting scales.






Activity 5.1: From raw scores to IQ and SAT scales





A tutorial keeping one test-score distribution fixed while its aligned ruler changes from raw scores to z-scores, an IQ scale, and an SAT scale.




Here is a hypothetical test-score distribution with a mean of 70 and a standard deviation of 5. The marked score of 80 is ten points above the mean, or two standard deviations. We’ll keep this curve and the marker exactly where they are throughout. Only the rulers underneath them will change.


First, lay the \(z\)-score ruler under the raw-score ruler. The old mean of 70 lines up with 0, and each five-point interval on the old ruler lines up with one unit on the new one. So the marked score of 80 is also \(z=2\). On this scale, the mean is 0 and the standard deviation is 1.


To make an IQ-style scale, first set the new standard deviation to 15. Add a third ruler, starting with a copy of the \(z\)-scores, then multiply every number on this new ruler by 15. The mean remains 0, while the standard deviation becomes 15. The marked score changes from 2 to 30. The original and \(z\) rulers stay in place for comparison.


Now add 100 to every number on that lower ruler. Adding the same amount to every score changes the mean from 0 to 100 without changing the standard deviation of 15. The marked position is now labeled 80 on the original ruler, 2 on the \(z\) ruler, and 130 on the IQ-style ruler.


We can now put away the original and \(z\) rulers and move the IQ-style ruler into place as the x-axis. The curve hasn’t changed shape, and our marked score is still two standard deviations above the mean. We’re simply reading that same position as 130 on a scale with a mean of 100 and a standard deviation of 15.


For an SAT-style scale, let’s start again with the original scores. The IQ ruler fades away, and the original x-axis returns: mean 70, standard deviation 5, marked score 80. We’ll follow the same procedure, this time choosing a different standard deviation and mean.


First, bring back the \(z\)-score ruler. Just as before, 70 lines up with 0 and 80 lines up with 2. This common scale, with a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 1, is the starting point for our next transformation.


Add another copy of the \(z\) ruler underneath, then multiply every \(z\)-score by 100 on that new ruler. This changes its standard deviation from 1 to 100 while leaving its mean at 0. The marked \(z\)-score of 2 becomes 200. The two rulers above still show the original score of 80 and its \(z\)-score of 2.


Now add 500 to every score on the bottom ruler. The reporting mean becomes 500 and the standard deviation stays 100. The same position is now labeled 80 on the original ruler, 2 on the \(z\) ruler, and 700 on the SAT-style ruler.


Finally, put away the reference rulers and move the SAT-style ruler up to the x-axis. Our marked score is now 700, still two standard deviations above the mean. Both transformations kept the scores in the same relative positions; we just chose different numbers to describe those positions.

title: 5  \(z\)-Scores
text:
Using \(z\)-scores to identify unusual scores
Comparing scores from different scales is one use of \(z\)-scores. Another is asking whether a score seems unusual or extreme. As we learned in Chapter 4, the standard deviation quantifies a “typical” deviation from the mean. So in that general sense, a \(z\)-score of \(1\) or \(-1\) would be perfectly typical and expected. More extreme \(z\)-scores, like \(2\) or \(-2\) would be less typical (again, according to the standard deviation’s definition of typicality).
Consider again the fake movie ratings from Chapter 4. Figure 5.4 shows two of those sets of scores with \(z\)-score rulers added. (The third movie, for which all the ratings were exactly the same, had a standard deviation of zero, so it can’t be standardized: the \(z\) equation would have us divide by that SD of zero, so the answer would be undefined.)



Figure 5.4





Block histogram of sample ratings for The Good, the Bad and the Okay with aligned raw-score and z-score rulers.




Block histogram of sample ratings for The Polarizing Express with aligned raw-score and z-score rulers.






Notice that The Good, the Bad and the Okay had most scores near the mean of 5, with two extreme scores out on either end. On the \(z\) scale, those extreme scores are beyond \(z = \pm 1\). According to our rough definition, whereby \(|z| = 1\) is considered typical, that seems right; those outlying scores are atypical for that distribution. But notice also that there aren’t actually any scores at \(z = \pm 1\). The z-score tells us the distance from the mean; how common scores are around that position still depends on the distribution’s shape. For The Polarizing Express, on the other hand, every score is within one standard deviation of the mean, simply because the standard deviation is so large. When every score is far from the mean, they are all typical in that sense.
Note the subtlety here: typical doesn’t necessarily have to imply close to the mean. But that was an unusual case. For reasons we will discuss over the next couple of chapters, we will more often find ourselves dealing with situations more like the ratings for The Good, the Bad and the Okay, where most scores are clustered around the mean and a few are out on the extremes. There, the standard deviation—and therefore, \(z\)-scores—generally tells us both how far a score is from the mean and how unusual it is.

Reaction times and radioactive spiders
Let’s think about this using a silly but hopefully memorable example. You know the gist of Spider-Man’s origin story, right? A high school kid gets bitten by a radioactive spider and develops superpowers, including Spidey Sense™️: the ability to sense and react to things unusually quickly. But how quick is unusually quick? Just how fast would a kid have to be for us to consider it evidence of superpowers? We can use \(z\)-scores to help answer that question.



Figure 5.5: My son’s toy Spider-Man action figure: he’s a big Spidey fan. That’s what inspired the goofy reaction time example.






First, I’d like you to have a go at testing your reaction times. Head over to humanbenchmark.com’s reaction time test. You’ll do a simple little test where you click as soon as the color on screen changes. You’ll do a few trials then note your average reaction time in milliseconds. When you’re done, make a note of your time (in milliseconds) by answering this quiz.
What was your average reaction time, in milliseconds?Enter just the number, such as 284. There is no right or wrong answer
here; we’ll come back to your time once we have a distribution to
compare it with.Show hintShow answerCheck your workClear

Our interpretation depends on the reference distribution. The results page for the Human Benchmark reaction-time test reports a mean recorded click time of 284 milliseconds. The site doesn’t give a standard deviation, so for this example we’ll just pick a reasonable-sounding value of 50 milliseconds. We’ll also model the scores as normally distributed—with a single peak in the middle and tails extending symmetrically in both directions—even though in reality the data are actually somewhat positively skewed. (This is an example about radioactive spider bites, after all, so I don’t mind taking a little artistic license with the data.)


Normal curve of reaction times centered on 284 ms with standard deviation 50 ms; a vertical line marks Peter Parker's 159 ms far down in the lower tail.


With those assumptions in place, we can calculate Peter Parker’s \(z\)-score:
\[z = \frac{X - \mu}{\sigma} = \frac{159 - 284}{50} = -2.5\]
Under our assumed normal model, that location is pretty uncommon: it sits well down in the lower tail. Peter’s reaction time doesn’t look typical of this reference distribution. Maybe the spider bite really did change him. We’ll revisit and develop the idea of testing a hypothesis about unusual reaction times in Chapter 8.

Clinical psychology and OCD treatment
We’ll have more fun with spider bites in Chapter 8, but for a more realistic example, let’s turn to clinical psychology and the treatment of mental health problems. This one is based on a published study that developed the 20-item Dimensional Obsessive-Compulsive Scale (DOCS) and used it to measure symptoms before and after exposure and response prevention, a form of cognitive behavioral therapy (Abramowitz et al., 2010).
Suppose the researchers found that prior to receiving treatment, people with diagnosed OCD scored 30.25 on that scale, with a standard deviation of 14.89. So the untreated population \(\mu = 30.25\) with \(\sigma = 14.89\).
Now suppose that you’re a clinical psychologist with a patient who has just completed a course of CBT and scored \(15.49\) on the DOCS. Where would that score place the patient within the untreated population? How far below average is it?

title: 5  \(z\)-Scores
text:
Looking ahead
Those specific numbers I gave above came from the real study, but I deliberately misused them. In the actual research, \(15.49\) wasn’t one individual’s score, it was the average of a sample of 40 people who completed the DOCS scale after receiving treatment (and 30.25 was those same people’s average score before treatment, not a population parameter). I treated it as an individual score to give you another chance to calculate and interpret a lone observation converted to a \(z\)-score, but in real research we usually want to understand how typical or expected the sample as a whole is. One individual scoring lower on a measure of symptom severity might be suggestive that their treatment helped, but a sample of 40 people collectively scoring lower can provide more compelling evidence.
This brings us to the boundary between descriptive and inferential statistics. \(z\)-scores are an essential building block of the logic we’ll use to deal with samples, but we have more work to do before we can make real inferences about treatment effects. In Chapter 6, we’ll introduce more precise ways of thinking about probability and using \(z\)-scores to understand normally distributed scores, and then in Chapters 7 and 8 we’ll explore the tools that enable us to apply that understanding to samples.

title: 6  Probability
text:
A Brief History of Probability
In the previous chapter, we hinted at thinking probabilistically about extreme scores in a distribution. Here, we’ll go into that idea in more detail. We’ll think about what statisticians mean when they talk about probability and how we go about quantifying it. We’ll need to introduce some new terminology, including probability distributions, and then we’ll return to \(z\) scores and see how a normal distribution lets us attach precise probabilities to regions of scores.
People have been thinking about probability for a long time, at least in a broad sense. It’s a useful thing to be able to make predictions about an uncertain future. Can I kill this sabre-toothed tiger, or will it probably kill me first? How much crop should we plant to feed the group? For most of that history, there were no formal ways of articulating how probable something might be. The best people could do was offer rough verbal descriptions. Aristotle distinguished between things that are pretty much unpredictable (“the accidental”), certainties (“that which is always”), and “that which is for the most part”—things that happen with some predictability. “That honey-water is useful for a patient in a fever is true for the most part,” Aristotle wrote as an example (Aristotle, n.d., Book VI, sec. 2). Sometimes it might help, sometimes not: it’s not certain, but neither is it entirely unpredictable. It’s something in between, more or less probable.
But how much more or less? The idea of representing uncertainty with numbers and reasoning about it mathematically was a relatively recent development. One of the early inspirations came not from life-and-death decisions but from games of chance. For thousands of years people have been playing games using bits of animal bone — two-sided, coin-like worked and decorated pieces of bone, or astragali, the four-sided ankle bones of sheep and goats. Games played this way were so popular that some people even manufactured astragali out of clay, stone or glass.
According to the card describing this glass astragal at the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York, playing with them was so much fun that “knucklebones have been found in tombs where they must have been intended to help the deceased while away endless time.” (So I guess, in a way, it was a matter of life and death.)
Astragali have four faces stable enough to land on, but the faces aren’t the same size or shape, so the four results aren’t equally likely. Cubical dice offered a more regular alternative to the irregular animal bones. The example below, something like 4,000 years old, even has the convention of opposite sides adding to seven that modern dice follow. These regularly shaped dice proved appealing to gamblers, and eventually to mathematicians, because it meant they could count outcomes and reason about them in a consistent way.

Catan
To see how this kind of probabilistic thinking works, let’s think about a relatively recent game, Catan. It’s a board game played by rolling a pair of dice (not goat knucklebones, thankfully). The board consists of hexagonal terrain tiles, each producing a resource such as wood or grain. Resources are good, so you want to get as many as possible. (We’ll ignore the differences between resources and other complications of the game.)
Most tiles have a number token. Players place settlements at the corners where tiles meet, and every time the dice are rolled, a settlement gets a resource from each neighboring tile whose number matches the sum of the two dice. So choosing where to settle means choosing which sums will pay you for the rest of the game. Suppose you get to go first, and you just want the greatest chance of getting something on each roll. title: 6  Probability
text:
Defining Probability
Let’s lay out some technical terms now, so that we have the precise language we need to reason about whether you picked the best spot.
First, what exactly do we mean by probability? As you might expect, there are distinct schools of thought and intense disagreement, which I am happy to sidestep for the most part. In this book, we will take an approach based in the frequentist tradition, since it’s the one that has dominated the social sciences for most of their history. A probability, in the frequentist sense, is a number that describes what would happen if we could repeat something many times: the proportion of repetitions in which some event of interest would occur in the long run. Probabilities range from 0 to 1. A probability of .5 means that, in the long run, we would expect the event to occur about half the time.
Let’s think about some simple situations in which there are a small number of equally-likely outcomes that we can count. (Later, we’ll generalize the same ideas to situations where outcomes are not equally likely, and to continuous variables and models where counting individual outcomes no longer works.) We’ll need some terms:

An outcome is one elementary result of a chance process.
An event is the outcome or collection of outcomes we’re actually interested in.
The sample space is the set of all the possible outcomes.

We use a capital letter \(P\) to denote probability and put the event we’re interested in inside parentheses. So \(P(A)\) means the probability of Event A. When every outcome in the sample space is equally likely, we can find that probability by counting the outcomes in A and dividing by the total number of possible outcomes.
\[ P(A) = \frac{\text{number of outcomes in } A}{\text{total number of possible outcomes}} \]
If you flip a fair coin, for example, there are two possible outcomes, heads or tails. The entire sample space consists of those two outcomes. If we want to denote the probability of heads, one of those two equally likely outcomes, we would write \(P(\text{heads}) = 1/2 = .5\). (Effectively the event is the outcome; there’s only one outcome that gets you heads.) Likewise, we would write the probability of tails as \(P(\text{tails}) = 1/2 = .5\).
Similarly, if we roll a fair six-sided die, there are six equally likely outcomes in the sample space, the die’s faces, one through six. So the probability of rolling a six is \(P(6) = 1/6 \approx .17\).
Perhaps we’re interested in the event of rolling an even number on a single six-sided die. Now we have an event that can be produced by more than one outcome. There are three individual outcomes (2, 4, 6) that would constitute that event. So the probability of rolling an even number is \(P(\text{even}) = 3/6 = 1/2 = .5\).

Rolling Two Dice
The same logic applies to rolling multiple dice; the sample space just expands, and we have to be careful about how to count things. Something that tripped up some early gamblers is that we’re interested in the sum of the dice, like the probability of rolling a 7, but some sums can be arrived at in multiple ways.1 Did you notice the red and blue dice at the top of the chapter? Red landed on 3 and blue landed on 4, for a sum of 7. But what if red had instead landed on 4 and blue on 3? The total would have been 7 as well. We need to count all the different ways each die might land to give the various possible totals.
Assuming both dice are fair and neither die’s result affects the other’s, each of the six red results can be paired with each of the six blue results, giving \(6 \times 6 = 36\) equally likely outcomes. Table 6.1 shows them all: rows give the red die’s result; columns give the blue die’s result.

We can take the 36 sums in the table and draw a bar graph counting how often each value appears. Each bar in Figure 6.3 counts the entries in the table that give that total. A total of 2 appears only once, for example, while 7 appears six times.



Figure 6.3: Counts of the dice totals in the table of 36 possible outcomes.




Bar graph of counts among 36 possible ordered dice outcomes. Totals 2 through 12 have counts 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 5, 4, 3, 2, and 1.





Now let’s make a similar version of the graph, with a small mathematical change:



Figure 6.4: The same dice totals, with each count divided by 36 to give a probability.




Bar graph showing probabilities for the sum of two dice, rising from 1/36 for 2 to 6/36 for 7, then falling symmetrically to 1/36 for 12.





Did you notice the difference? We divided each count by the total, 36, to turn frequencies into proportions. The shape of the distribution is the same; only the vertical scale changes.
It’s a small mathematical tweak but a bigger conceptual leap. Rather than counting every outcome in the sample space once, as in Figure 6.3, each bar tells us the long-run proportion of future rolls on which that total would occur. These probabilities form a probability distribution. It shows every possible value of the variable and the probability attached to each one. The counts in Figure 6.3 add up to 36; the probabilities in Figure 6.4 add up to 1.
We can use it to predict frequencies: over 100 rolls, for example, we’d expect a total of 7 about \(100 \times (6/36) \approx 17\) times. (If we actually roll the dice 100 times we might not get exactly that many sevens; we’re describing what to expect from the chance process, not a strict guarantee. More on this a little later.)
One more thing to note. If we’re interested in two or more mutually exclusive events, meaning they cannot happen together on the same roll, we can add their probabilities to find the probability of one or the other. For example, the probability of rolling a sum of 5 or 6 is:
\[ P(5 \text{ or } 6) = P(5) + P(6) = \frac{4}{36} + \frac{5}{36} = \frac{9}{36} \approx .25 \]

Back to Catan
